nature-clim-149.title: Climate change mitigation: cutting the cause
nature-clim-149.text: To hold warming to 1.5 °C, 2022 assessments said, global emissions must peak before 2025 and fall about 43% by 2030. Climate change mitigation is action to limit the greenhouse gases in the atmosphere that cause climate change. It is also called decarbonization. The IPCC defines it as a human intervention to reduce emissions or enhance the sinks of greenhouse gases. The main actions are saving energy and replacing fossil fuels with clean energy. Changing land use and removing CO2 are secondary strategies. Measures fall into four types: sustainable energy and transport, energy conservation, sustainable agriculture and green industry, and enhancing sinks and carbon removal. Solar and wind can replace fossil fuels at the lowest cost of the renewable options. Some processes resist, and air travel and cement production are among the hardest to decarbonize. The gap remains wide. Adopted policies would still lead to about 2.7 °C of warming by 2100, well above the Paris Agreement goal. Mitigation is often seen as a burden to share. It can also be an opportunity for industrial development and exports.

nature-clim-143.title: Carbon sequestration: putting carbon away
nature-clim-143.text: Using all of Earth's geologic storage would limit warming by only 0.7 °C, a 2025 study found. Storage is no cure-all, yet it is a real tool. Carbon sequestration is the storing of carbon in a carbon pool, a place in the Earth system where carbon stays for a period of time. By lowering the carbon dioxide in the air, it helps manage the carbon cycle and limit climate change. It comes in two main types. Biologic sequestration, or biosequestration, relies on plants, which take carbon dioxide from the air as they grow and bind it into biomass. People can speed this up through land use and farming. But stores such as forests may be temporary, since fires, disease, economic pressure and politics can release the carbon. Geologic sequestration lasts far longer. Injecting CO2 underground, or turning it into carbonate salts, locks carbon away for thousands to millions of years. Within carbon capture and storage, sequestration is the storage step.

nature-clim-136.title: The carbon budget: how much CO2 is left to burn
nature-clim-136.text: From 1750 to 2019, humanity emitted about 2390 gigatonnes of CO2. How much more can it afford? A carbon budget is the largest total of carbon dioxide that can still be emitted, added up over time, while keeping warming below a chosen limit. It is also called an emissions budget, quota or allowable emissions. Counted from the pre-industrial year 1750 it is the total budget, and from a recent date the remaining budget. The idea works because warming rises almost in a straight line with cumulative CO2 emissions. The warming does not depend on where emissions come from and depends little on when. Estimates depend on the temperature target, the chosen probability of staying below it, and how far other greenhouse gases are cut. A 2023 update found 250 GtCO2 left from January 2023 for a 50% chance of staying below 1.5 °C. That is about 6 years of current emissions. For 2 degrees, it gave 1220 GtCO2, about 30 years.

nature-clim-208.title: The low-carbon economy
nature-clim-208.text: Switching to lower-emission technologies often pays back within 0.5–5 years. A low-carbon economy absorbs as much greenhouse gas as it emits, or more broadly produces far lower emissions. Related terms include green economy and decarbonized economy, with 'carbon' standing for all greenhouse gases. Getting there means cutting emissions in every sector through renewables, efficiency, electric vehicles, heat pumps and climate-smart agriculture. It needs energy policies and incentives such as emissions trading and carbon taxes. Benefits reach ecosystems, trade, jobs, health, energy security and competitiveness. Workers in carbon-intensive industries are more likely to lose jobs, while renewables and building renovation create new ones. The obstacle is a free-rider problem: each country gains from others' mitigation but loses by going low-carbon alone.

nature-clim-185.title: Carbon capture and storage: catching CO2 at the chimney
nature-clim-185.text: As of 2023, carbon capture and storage (CCS) caught about 45 million tonnes of CO2 a year, around 0.1% of global emissions. CCS separates carbon dioxide from industrial sources before it reaches the air and moves it to long-term storage, usually deep underground. Capture usually passes exhaust through an amine solvent that binds CO2. Around 80% of captured CO2 is used for enhanced oil recovery, pumped into oil fields to push out more oil. So CCS is also called carbon capture, utilization and storage (CCUS). Cost is the sticking point. Capture costs US$15–25 per tonne for concentrated streams such as gas processing. Dilute streams from power, cement and steel plants cost US$40–120. Many other ways to cut emissions cost under US$20 per tonne. Because designs are site-specific, learning-by-doing brings costs down only slowly. The research literature gives CCS a small but critical role. Fossil fuel companies, meanwhile, promote it to extend the fossil era. CCS therefore remains politically divisive, with open disagreement over its cost-effectiveness and whether it prolongs fossil fuel use.

nature-clim-178.title: Biochar: charcoal that feeds the soil
nature-clim-178.text: Long before Europeans arrived, Amazonians smoldered farm waste into charcoal, creating soils later settlers called terra preta. Biochar is that kind of charcoal: made by heating biomass with little oxygen, and meant for soil and other organic uses. The process, pyrolysis, yields solid biochar, liquid bio-oil and syngas. In soil it can improve aeration and fertility, reduce nutrient leaching and acidity, and cut greenhouse gas emissions. It helps degraded tropical soils more than temperate ones. Too much, or the wrong feedstock, can harm soil life, change pH and raise salinity. Biochar is so stable that it can stay in soils for thousands of years, which underlies biochar carbon removal. A 1–2% share in concrete also cuts emissions from cement.

nature-clim-153.title: Co-benefits: what cutting emissions also buys
nature-clim-153.text: Fossil-fuel air pollution is estimated to kill over 5 million people a year as of 2019. Cutting emissions would also cut that toll. Co-benefits are the side benefits of mitigation beyond slowing climate change, such as cleaner air, better health, jobs and energy security. They are also called ancillary benefits. Replacing coal plants with renewables can, in some cases, more than double the jobs per megawatt of capacity. Countries that import energy can gain independence and supply security by building renewables. Yet the IPCC noted in 2007 that decision-makers often neglect co-benefits and do not quantify or monetize them. Counting them properly can change decisions about when and how much to mitigate.

nature-clim-150.title: Demand-side mitigation: wanting less carbon
nature-clim-150.text: The richest 10% of people cause about half of all lifestyle emissions. Demand-side mitigation cuts emissions by reducing demand for the goods and services that cause them, through behavior, infrastructure and end-use technology. Examples include eating less meat, building good public transport and insulating houses. High-impact personal actions include flying less, avoiding petrol cars, eating mainly plants and electrifying homes. Together, demand-side solutions could cut global greenhouse gas emissions by 40% to 70% by 2050 while improving well-being.

nature-clim-160.title: Mitigation sector by sector
nature-clim-160.text: Emissions come from every corner of the economy, so cuts are grouped by where they happen: buildings, transport, industry, and agriculture, forestry and land use. Buildings account for 23% of global energy-related CO2 emissions. About half their energy goes to heating space and water. Heat pumps are a strong tool there, because a modern one moves about three to five times more heat energy than the electricity it uses. Transport causes 15% of emissions. Public transport, cycling, electric vehicles and rail help cut them. Counting direct and indirect emissions, industry is the largest emitter. Electrification, green hydrogen and circular economy measures, which keep materials in use, can reduce its share. Agriculture and forestry cause almost 20% of emissions, and cattle alone produce 21% of global methane. Each sector therefore needs its own mix of measures.

nature-clim-159.title: Protecting the sinks that soak up carbon
nature-clim-159.text: The Stern Review said in 2007 that curbing deforestation was a highly cost-effective way to cut emissions. Preserving and enhancing carbon sinks means managing Earth's natural sinks so they keep or increase their ability to take CO2 from the air and store it durably. Globally the two most important sinks are vegetation and the ocean. Examples are preventing deforestation and restoring ecosystems by reforestation. Ecosystem restoration and less land conversion are among the tools that can cut the most emissions before 2030. The economic potential of forest and ecosystem measures is 4.2 to 7.4 GtCO2-eq per year.

nature-clim-144.title: Biological sequestration: letting plants do the work
nature-clim-144.text: Wetlands cover only 5–8% of the world's land, yet they hold 20–30% of its soil carbon. That makes them prized stores in biological carbon sequestration: capturing and storing atmospheric carbon dioxide through living processes, mainly plant growth, that people keep up and enhance. It works by raising photosynthesis through land uses such as reforestation and sustainable forest management. Forests act as land carbon sinks, storing carbon in roots, stems, branches and leaves. The process also runs in reverse. Converting natural land to cropland cuts soil organic carbon by about 30–40%. Keeping natural land intact is therefore part of the strategy, alongside growing new forests.

nature-clim-145.title: Geological sequestration: storing CO2 a kilometer down
nature-clim-145.text: Earth holds nearly 12,000 GtCO2 of theoretical underground storage space, but 2025 research found only 1,460 GtCO2 of it risk-free. Geological carbon sequestration stores carbon dioxide deep underground in depleted oil and gas fields, saline formations, or coal beds that cannot be mined. Captured CO2 is compressed to about 100 bar, piped to the site and injected around 1 km deep. There it can stay for hundreds to millions of years. A good site has porous, permeable rock such as sandstone, sealed under a tight cap rock such as shale. The risks are CO2 leaking up along faults, and earthquakes triggered by too much pressure. Storage itself is cheap. Without capture and transport, it can cost below US$10 per tonne where onshore storage is available. The expensive part of carbon capture and storage is catching the gas, not burying it.

nature-clim-202.title: Greenhouse gas inventories: national emission ledgers
nature-clim-202.text: Almost every country is a party to the Paris Agreement, which requires regular inventories of the emissions produced on its territory. A greenhouse gas inventory records the greenhouse gases emitted, and removed by carbon sinks, in a country, region or organization. Counting removals sets it apart from other air emission inventories. Parties to the UNFCCC and the Kyoto Protocol must submit annual inventories of human emissions and removals. The simplest method multiplies an amount of activity, such as fuel burned, by an 'emission factor'. Scientists feed inventories into atmospheric models, and policy makers use them to design and track emission cuts.

nature-clim-175.title: Stranded assets: investments that die young
nature-clim-175.text: When markets or rules change, a power plant or oil field can stop earning a return long before the end of its expected economic life. The IEA calls such investments stranded assets. More generally, a stranded asset has suffered an unexpected or early write-down, loss of value, or conversion into a liability. Stranding is part of the 'creative destruction' of growth and innovation. It can also carry risks for the whole financial system. Climate change is expected to sharply increase stranded assets in carbon-intensive industries, with ripple effects through the world economy. That is why the term matters in financial risk management.

nature-clim-209.title: Low-carbon electricity
nature-clim-209.text: In 2020 almost 40% of global electricity came from low-carbon sources: about 10% nuclear, almost 10% wind and solar, and around 20% hydro and other renewables. Low-carbon electricity has far lower lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions than fossil fuel power. Sources include wind, solar, nuclear and most hydropower. Fossil plants count only when fitted with carbon capture, and very little power comes from them, mostly because capture is costly. Moving to low-carbon power is among the most important actions to limit climate change.

nature-clim-161.title: What holds mitigation back
nature-clim-161.text: Only 0.12% of climate research funding goes to the social science of mitigation. That gap is one of many barriers to cutting emissions, the individual, institutional and market obstacles in the way. Finance is a major barrier for land-based options, and accounting for carbon removal is an economic one. Developing countries face a shortage of capital, which grew more costly in the early 2020s.

nature-clim-157.title: Pledges versus warming
nature-clim-157.text: In November 2021, Climate Action Tracker projected 2.7 °C of warming by 2100 under current policies. Countries' announced targets tell a better story on paper. If all were met, warming would peak at 1.9 °C and fall to 1.8 °C by 2100. The gap lies in delivery: only the EU, UK, Chile and Costa Rica had detailed official plans for their 2030 targets.

nature-clim-158.title: Coal-to-gas switching: a short-term fix
nature-clim-158.text: For electricity, burning natural gas gives about half the emissions of coal, and for heat about two-thirds. Replacing coal with gas can therefore cut emissions in the short term. But methane leaking during extraction and transport can cancel out the gain. Gas is no path to net zero, and new gas infrastructure risks carbon lock-in and stranded assets.

nature-clim-152.title: The low-carbon diet
nature-clim-152.text: Food makes up the largest share of consumption-based emissions, nearly 20% of the global carbon footprint. A low-carbon diet means eating fewer animal products and more plant-based food. Widespread vegetarian diets could cut food-related emissions by 63% by 2050. Land would be freed too. Returning land used for animal farming to nature could sequester 100 billion tonnes of CO2 by 2100.

nature-clim-154.title: When mitigation does harm
nature-clim-154.text: Clean energy needs metals and minerals, and mining them can threaten conservation areas. Some mitigation measures carry such harms and risks, including damage to biodiversity. Yet dwelling on risks has its own danger. Because people weigh possible losses more than benefits, focusing on the downsides can produce deadlock.

nature-clim-156.title: Who should cut, and who should pay?
nature-clim-156.text: Responsibility for cutting emissions must be divided among regions, income groups and sectors, and so must its costs. Proposed principles include egalitarianism, basic needs, proportionality and the polluter-pays principle. 'Equal per capita entitlements' allocate emissions by population, or by population while also counting historical emissions.

nature-clim-137.title: Splitting the world's carbon budget
nature-clim-137.text: If the world can emit only so much more CO2, which country gets how much? Dividing the carbon budget requires value judgments about fairness. Nations differ in population, industrialization, past emissions and ability to cut, so scientists apply principles of equity. Under 'common but differentiated responsibilities', countries that emitted more in the past or are richer get smaller budgets. The egalitarian principle shares budgets by population. That raises an awkward question: do individuals have a right to pollute? Grandfathering shares budgets according to each nation's emissions in a base year. It was used under the Kyoto Protocol and the early EU emissions trading system, and it favors developed countries. Recent work argues that grandfathering is not a standard of equity at all, because it builds in biases against poorer states. Scholars still disagree about which principle should divide the budget.

nature-clim-147.title: Burying wood to lock away carbon
nature-clim-147.text: Fossil fuels formed from buried plant matter. Biomass burial copies the trick, storing carbon by burying wood or other plant matter where it cannot rot. Its global potential is estimated at 10 ± 5 GtC per year, highest in tropical forests. It is also cheap. A 2008 estimate put wood burial at US$50 per tonne of carbon, much cheaper than capturing power-plant emissions.

nature-clim-148.title: Pumping CO2 into the deep sea: an abandoned idea
nature-clim-148.text: Injecting carbon dioxide directly into the deep ocean was once proposed as a way to store it for some centuries. Interest faded after about 2001. Effects on marine life were unknown, costs were high, and nobody could be sure how long the carbon would stay. The IPCC listed the option in 2005, but by 2014 it no longer mentioned ocean storage.

nature-clim-146.title: Mineral carbonation: turning CO2 into stone
nature-clim-146.text: Much of Earth's limestone formed as carbon dioxide slowly reacted with rock over geologic time. Mineral carbonation does the same on purpose, reacting CO2 with metal oxides such as magnesium or calcium oxide to make solid carbonate minerals. Heat, pressure, catalysts or grinding can speed it up, but they need extra energy. Another route works underground: CO2 dissolved in water and injected into hot basalt turns into solid carbonate.

nature-clim-207.title: Learning-by-doing: getting better with practice
nature-clim-207.text: Learning-by-doing was first measured in World War II bomber production. Costs fell with the total number of bombers ever built, not with how many were built at once. The idea is that productivity rises through practice, self-improvement and small innovations. A factory, for example, can produce more by learning to use its equipment better, with no extra workers or capital. These learning economies grow with cumulative production, the pattern of the experience curve. It explains the steep, non-linear cost falls in semiconductors and solar PV. Kenneth Arrow built it into endogenous growth theory, and Robert Lucas used it to explain increasing returns to human capital.

nature-clim-203.title: Counting emissions where made or where consumed
nature-clim-203.text: In Norway, 69% of CO2 comes from making goods for export. Under production-based accounting, such a country could meet its targets just by exporting less. There are two main ways to count a nation's emissions. Production-based accounting counts emissions made on its territory, including exports but excluding imports. Consumption-based accounting counts those caused by what it consumes, imports included. Policy favors the production method because it is easier to measure, but it misses emissions embodied in trade. The consumption method traces products through global supply chains with multi-regional input-output models. It is more uncertain, needs more data and depends on international cooperation. The literature disagrees which method is fairer and better for policy, and some propose sharing responsibility.

openers.mitigation-and-carbon-removal: Limiting the greenhouse gases that cause climate change, often called decarbonization, means two kinds of work. One is cutting emissions, sector by sector across buildings, transport, industry and land, and by reducing demand for the goods and services that cause them. The other is storing carbon: in forests and other natural sinks, as charcoal in soil, or as captured carbon dioxide pumped deep underground. A carbon budget sets the stakes, the total humanity can still emit while keeping warming below a chosen limit. Cutting emissions also brings side benefits, such as cleaner air, better health, jobs and energy security.
